hints: Link the named unit of charge to both a current value and a time interval.
State the charge transferred when a current of one ampere flows for one second.
walkthrough: Current is the rate at which charge is transferred.
A current of one ampere transfers one coulomb of charge each second.
Therefore, one coulomb is the charge transferred when a current of one ampere flows for one second.

ai_rubric.observable: States that a coulomb is an ampere second, or the charge transferred by one ampere in one second.

hints: Consider a length l of the wire and use its cross-sectional area to find the volume containing the moving charge carriers.
Relate the charge through that length to current and time, then replace l/t by the drift speed.
walkthrough: A length l of wire has volume Al.
With n charge carriers per unit volume, this length contains nAl carriers.
Each carrier has charge e, so the total charge in this length is Q = nAle.
The current is I = Q/t, so I = nAle/t.
The average drift speed is v = l/t, giving I = nAve.
Rearrange to obtain v = I/(nAe).

ai_rubric.observable: Forms the carrier charge in a length l as Q = nAle, or an equivalent expression.
Uses I = Q/t and identifies l/t as the drift speed.
Obtains I = nAve and rearranges it to v = I/(nAe).

hints: The resistors are in series, so the current is the same in Y and Z; the wires also have the same carrier number density and carrier charge.
Use v = I/(nAe), then compare only the cross-sectional areas of the wires.
walkthrough: For each wire, v = I/(nAe).
Y and Z are in series, so they carry the same current I. Their material is the same, so n and e are also the same.
Thus v is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A.
Wire Z has diameter 2d, so A_Z = π(2d)²/4 = πd² = 4A_Y.
Therefore v_Y/v_Z = A_Z/A_Y = 4.

ai_rubric.observable: Forms the drift-speed ratio from I/(nAe) for the two wires.
Shows that the ratio reduces to A_Z/A_Y and evaluates the area ratio as 4.

hints: The wires have the same material, so use R = ρL/A and compare how length and cross-sectional area change.
Doubling a wire's diameter makes its cross-sectional area four times larger.
walkthrough: For wire Y, R_Y = ρl/A.
Wire Z has length 2l and diameter 2d, so its cross-sectional area is 4A.
Thus R_Z = ρ(2l)/(4A) = ρl/(2A).
The ratio is R_Y/R_Z = (ρl/A)/(ρl/(2A)) = 2.
Therefore the resistance of Y divided by the resistance of Z is 2.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses R = ρL/A, or an equivalent expression for the wire resistance.
Accounts for the doubled length and fourfold area of Z to obtain R_Y/R_Z = 2.

hints: Y and Z are in series and the resistance ratio from part (ii) is R_Y:R_Z = 2:1.
Use the resistance fraction for Y to find its share of the 12 V supply.
walkthrough: From part (ii), the resistance ratio is R_Y:R_Z = 2:1.
The total series resistance is therefore three equal resistance parts, of which Y accounts for two.
Use the potential-divider relation: V_Y = 12 × R_Y/(R_Y + R_Z).

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the series resistance ratio in a potential-divider relation, or an equivalent current-and-Ohm's-law route.
Obtains a potential difference across Y of 8.0 V.

hints: Y and Z are in series, so they carry the same current.
Use P = I²R and the resistance ratio from part (ii).
walkthrough: Y and Z are in series, so both carry the same current I.
Use P = I²R for each resistor.
Thus P_Y / P_Z = (I²R_Y) / (I²R_Z) = R_Y / R_Z.
From part (ii), R_Y / R_Z = 2, so P_Y / P_Z = 2.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses a valid electrical-power relationship to obtain P_Y / P_Z = 2.
